title: Chapter 64 — Stubb’s Supper
paragraphs: Stubb's whale had been killed some way off from the ship. There was a dead calm, so we formed a tandem of three boats and began the slow job of towing the trophy back to the Pequod. Hour after hour we eighteen men, with our thirty-six arms and one hundred and eighty thumbs and fingers, labored at that inert, sluggish corpse in the sea, and it seemed hardly to budge at all except at long intervals — plenty of proof of how enormous a mass we were moving. On the great canal of Hang-Ho, or whatever they call it, in China, four or five laborers on the towpath can haul a bulky loaded junk at a mile an hour; but this grand argosy of ours forged heavily along as if its hold were packed with pig-lead.

Darkness fell, but three lights hung up and down the Pequod's main-rigging dimly showed us the way; and as we drew nearer we saw Ahab lowering one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. He looked blankly at the heaving whale for a moment, gave the usual orders for making it fast for the night, and then handed his lantern to a seaman and went off into the cabin, not coming forward again until morning.

Captain Ahab had shown his usual activity, if you can call it that, in directing the chase of this whale; but now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, impatience, or despair seemed to be at work in him — as if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was still to be killed, and that even if a thousand other whales were brought to his ship, not one of them would bring his grand, monomaniac goal one jot closer. Soon, from the noise on the Pequod's decks, you would have thought all hands were getting ready to drop anchor in the deep; heavy chains are being dragged along the deck and shoved rattling out through the portholes. But those clanking links are meant to moor not the ship but the vast corpse itself. Tied by the head to the stern and by the tail to the bows, the whale now lies with its black hull close against the vessel's; and seen through the dark of night, which hid the spars and rigging overhead, the two — ship and whale — looked yoked together like colossal bullocks, one lying down while the other stands.*

*A little item may as well be told here. The strongest and most reliable hold the ship has on the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes, or tail; and since that part, from its greater density, is relatively heavier than any other (except the side-fins), its flexibility, even in death, makes it sink low beneath the surface, so that you cannot reach it by hand from the boat to put the chain around it. But this difficulty is ingeniously overcome: a small, strong line is prepared with a wooden float at its outer end and a weight in its middle, while the other end is made fast to the ship. By skillful management the wooden float is made to rise on the other side of the mass, so that, the line having now girdled the whale, the chain is easily made to follow; and being slipped along the body, it is at last locked fast around the smallest part of the tail, where it joins the broad flukes or lobes.

If moody Ahab was now all stillness, at least as far as could be known on deck, Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, showed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. He was in such an unaccustomed bustle that the sober Starbuck, his official superior, quietly left the sole management of affairs to him for the time being. One small contributing cause of all this liveliness in Stubb was soon made strangely plain. Stubb was a high liver; he was somewhat intemperately fond of the whale as a thing flavorful to his palate.
"A steak, a steak, before I sleep! You, Daggoo! Overboard you go, and cut me one from his small!"

It should be known here that although these wild fishermen do not, as a general rule, follow the great military maxim of making the enemy pay the running expenses of the war (at least not before realizing the proceeds of the voyage), yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine relish for that particular part of the Sperm Whale that Stubb named, which takes in the tapering end of the body.

Around midnight the steak was cut and cooked, and by the light of two sperm-oil lanterns Stubb stood up stoutly to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as though the capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only one feasting on whale meat that night. Thousands upon thousands of sharks, swarming around the dead leviathan, mixed their mumblings with his chewing as they feasted noisily on its fat. The few sleepers in their bunks below were often startled by the sharp slap of the sharks' tails against the hull, only a few inches from their hearts. If you peered over the side you could just make them out (having heard them first), wallowing in the sullen black water and rolling onto their backs as they scooped huge round chunks the size of a human head out of the whale. This particular feat of the shark seems almost miraculous. How they manage to gouge such symmetrical mouthfuls out of a surface that looks impossible to bite into remains part of the universal problem of all things. The mark they leave on the whale is best compared to the hollow a carpenter makes when countersinking for a screw.

Amid all the smoking horror and devilry of a sea-fight, sharks can be seen gazing longingly up at the ship's decks, like hungry dogs around a table where red meat is being carved, ready to gulp down every dead man thrown to them. While the valiant butchers at the deck-table are cannibally carving one another's live flesh with gilded, tasseled carving-knives, the sharks, with their jewel-hilted mouths, are carving away quarrelsomely under the table at the dead meat — and if you turned the whole affair upside down it would still be much the same thing, that is, a shocking, sharkish business all round. Sharks are also the unfailing outriders of every slave ship crossing the Atlantic, trotting methodically alongside, handy in case a parcel needs carrying somewhere or a dead slave needs a decent burial. And one or two other such cases could be listed, concerning the set times, places, and occasions when sharks gather most sociably and feast most hilariously. Yet there is no conceivable time or occasion when you will find them in such countless numbers, or in gayer and more jovial spirits, than around a dead sperm whale moored at night to a whaleship at sea. If you have never seen that sight, then hold off deciding whether devil-worship is proper and whether it is wise to keep on the good side of the devil.
But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the mumblings of the banquet going on so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

"Cook, cook! — where's that old Fleece?" he cried at length, spreading his legs still wider as if to form a more secure base for his supper, and at the same time stabbing his fork into the dish as if it were a lance. "Cook, you cook! — sail this way, cook!"

The old black, in no great glee at having already been roused from his warm hammock at a most unseasonable hour, came shambling out of his galley. Like many old blacks, he had something wrong with his knee-pans, which he did not keep as well scoured as his other pans. This old Fleece, as they called him, came shuffling and limping along, propping up his step with his tongs, a clumsy pair made of straightened iron hoops. This old Ebony floundered forward and, as ordered, stopped dead on the far side of Stubb's sideboard. Then, with both hands folded in front of him and resting on his two-legged cane, he bent his arched back over still further, tilting his head to one side at the same time so as to bring his better ear into play.

"Cook," said Stubb, quickly lifting a rather reddish morsel to his mouth, "don't you think this steak is rather overdone? You've been beating this steak too much, cook; it's too tender. Don't I always say that to be good, a whale steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side — don't you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a racket they're kicking up! Cook, go and talk to them; tell them they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. Here, take this lantern," snatching one from his sideboard; "now then, go and preach to them!"

Sullenly, old Fleece took the lantern he was offered and limped across the deck to the bulwarks. Then, holding his light low over the sea with one hand to get a good look at his congregation, he solemnly waved his tongs with the other, leaned far out over the side, and began to address the sharks in a mumbling voice, while Stubb crept softly up behind him and overheard everything that was said.

"Fellow-critters: I'se ordered here to say dat you must stop dat damn noise dere. You hear? Stop dat damn smackin' of de lip! Massa Stubb say dat you can fill your damn bellies up to de hatches, but by Gor! you must stop dat damn racket!"
"Cook," Stubb cut in here, with a sudden slap on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"
"Who dat? Den preach to him yourself," sullenly turning to go.
"No, cook. Go on, go on."
"Well, den, beloved fellow-critters:" —
"Right!" exclaimed Stubb approvingly. "Coax them into it. Try that." And Fleece continued.

"Though you is all sharks, and by natur' very voracious, yet I say to you, fellow-critters, dat dat voraciousness — 'top dat damn slappin' of de tail! How you tink to hear, s'pose you keep up such a damn slappin' and bitin' dere?"
"Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like a gentleman."
Once more the sermon proceeded.

"Your voraciousness, fellow-critters, I don't blame you so much for; dat is natur', and can't be helped; but to govern dat wicked natur', dat is de point. You is sharks, certain; but if you govern de shark in you, why den you be angel; for all angel is nothin' more dan de shark well governed. Now, look here, brethren, just try once to be civil, a-helpin' yourselves from dat whale. Don't be tearin' de blubber out of your neighbor's mouth, I say. Ain't one shark got as good a right as de other to dat whale? And, by Gor, none of you has de right to dat whale; dat whale belong to somebody else. I know some of you has very big mouth, bigger dan others; but den de big mouths sometimes has de small bellies; so dat de bigness of de mouth is not to swallow wid, but to bite off de blubber for de small fry of sharks, dat can't get into de crush to help demselves."
"Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb. "That's Christianity. Go on."

"No use goin' on; de damn villains will keep a-jostlin' and slappin' each other, Massa Stubb; dey don't hear one word; no use a-preachin' to such damn gluttons as you call 'em, till dere bellies is full, and dere bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get 'em full, dey won't hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear nothin' at all, no more, for ever and ever."
"Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion. So give the benediction, Fleece, and I'll get back to my supper."
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice and cried —
"Cussed fellow-critters! Kick up de damnedest row as ever you can; fill your damn bellies till dey bust — and den die."
"Now, cook," said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan, "stand just where you stood before, there, across from me, and pay particular attention."
"All 'tention," said Fleece, again stooping over his tongs in the desired position.
"Well," said Stubb, helping himself generously meanwhile, "I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?"
"What dat do wid de steak?" said the old black, testily.
"Silence! How old are you, cook?"
"'Bout ninety, dey say," he muttered gloomily.

"And you have lived in this world close to one hundred years, cook, and don't know yet how to cook a whale steak?" — rapidly swallowing another mouthful at the last word, so that it seemed a continuation of the question. "Where were you born, cook?"
"'Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin' over de Roanoke."
"Born on a ferryboat! That's odd, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!"
"Didn't I say de Roanoke country?" he cried sharply.
"No, you didn't, cook. But I'll tell you what I'm getting at, cook. You must go home and be born all over again. You don't know how to cook a whale steak yet."
"Bress my soul if I cook anoder one," he growled angrily, turning around to leave.

"Come back, cook — here, hand me those tongs — now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak is cooked as it should be? Take it, I say" — holding the tongs toward him — "take it, and taste it."
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old negro muttered, "Best cooked steak I ever taste; joosy, very joosy."
"Cook," said Stubb, squaring himself once more, "do you belong to the church?"
"Passed one once in Cape-Down," said the old man sullenly.

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape Town, where you no doubt overheard a holy parson addressing his listeners as his beloved fellow-creatures — have you, cook! And yet you come here and tell me such a dreadful lie as you just did, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go, cook?"
"Go to bed very soon," he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
"Halt! Heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It's an awful question. Now what's your answer?"
"When dis old black man dies," said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and manner, "he hisself won't go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him."
"Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?"
"Up dere," said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head and keeping them there very solemnly.
"So you expect to go up to our main-top when you die, do you, cook? But don't you know that the higher you climb, the colder it gets? The main-top, eh?"
"Didn't say dat at all," said Fleece, sulking again.

"You said up there, didn't you? And now look for yourself and see where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole (the opening through a mast's top platform that novice climbers use), cook; but no, no, cook, you don't get there unless you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a ticklish business, but it must be done, or else it's no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do you hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap the other on top of your heart when I'm giving my orders, cook. What! That your heart, there? — that's your gizzard! Aloft! Aloft! — that's it — now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention."
"All 'tention," said the old black, placing both hands as requested, vainly wriggling his grizzled head as if trying to get both ears in front at one and the same time.

"Well then, cook, you see, this whale steak of yours was so very bad that I've put it out of sight as fast as I could; you see that, don't you? Well, from now on, when you cook another whale steak for my private table here, the capstan, I'll tell you what to do so you don't spoil it by overcooking. Hold the steak in one hand and show a live coal to it with the other; once that's done, serve it up. Hear me? And tomorrow, cook, when we're cutting in the fish, make sure you're standing by to get the tips of his fins; have them pickled. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. There, now you can go."
But Fleece had hardly gotten three steps away when he was called back.
"Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Make a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."

"Wish, by Gor, whale eat him, 'stead of him eat whale. I'm bressed if he ain't more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself," muttered the old man, limping away; and with this sage outburst he went to his hammock.
